title: Phishing (part 1)
starter: Think of a message you have received that looked suspicious. What made you doubt it? If you have never had one, describe what you would look for.
starterAnswer: Accept any sensible attempt: this is a hook, not an assessment.
Look for the vocabulary from the lesson objectives appearing in students' own words.
Students who are stuck should still write something: the experience will correct it.
starterNote: Take two or three answers, then leave it open. Come back to it in the plenary, when they can answer it properly.

stations.name: What is phishing?
facts: An online fraud technique: fake messages designed to trick people into giving away personal information.
The message pretends to come from a trustworthy organisation, such as a bank or a school.
It's a form of social engineering: it targets people, not software.
stations.challenge: Write the exam definition of phishing in your own words.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: An online fraud technique: fake messages designed to trick people into giving away personal information.
Also credit: The message pretends to come from a trustworthy organisation, such as a bank or a school.

questions.a: Fraudulent messages that trick people into disclosing personal information by pretending to be trustworthy

questions.q: Why is phishing called social engineering?
questions.a: It manipulates people rather than attacking the technology

stations.name: What attackers gain
facts: Usernames and passwords, which open email, banking and school accounts.
Bank and card details, used for fraud or sold on.
A way into an organisation's network, by stealing a staff login.
stations.challenge: What could an attacker do with a teacher's school password?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Usernames and passwords, which open email, banking and school accounts.
Also credit: Bank and card details, used for fraud or sold on.

questions.q: What is the main aim of a phishing attack?
questions.a: To get the victim to hand over information such as passwords or bank details

questions.q: Why do attackers target staff logins at a company?
questions.a: One stolen login can give access to the whole network

stations.name: Spot the signs
facts: Check the sender's address, not just the display name.
Look for urgency or threats: 'act now or your account will be closed'.
Generic greetings, spelling mistakes and odd formatting are clues.
Unexpected attachments or links asking you to log in.
stations.challenge: List four signs that an email might be phishing.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Check the sender's address, not just the display name.
Also credit: Look for urgency or threats: 'act now or your account will be closed'.

questions.q: Which of these are warning signs of phishing? Select all that apply.
questions.a: The sender's address doesn't match the organisation; The message threatens that your account will close today; A generic greeting such as 'Dear customer'; A link that goes to an unfamiliar web address

stations.name: Check the link
facts: Hover over a link to see where it really goes.
Attackers use lookalike addresses, such as barclays-secure-login.com.
A padlock only means the connection is encrypted; it doesn't mean the site is honest.
stations.challenge: Which of the addresses on the wall is genuine, and how can you tell?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Hover over a link to see where it really goes.
Also credit: Attackers use lookalike addresses, such as barclays-secure-login.com.

questions.q: Which address is most likely to be genuine for a bank called Bank?
Does a padlock in the address bar mean a site is safe?
questions.a: No: it only means the connection is encrypted

stations.name: Targeted phishing
facts: Spear phishing targets one person, using details about them to look convincing.
Whaling targets senior staff, such as a head teacher or finance director.
Smishing uses text messages and vishing uses phone calls.
stations.challenge: Why is spear phishing more likely to succeed than a mass email?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Spear phishing targets one person, using details about them to look convincing.
Also credit: Whaling targets senior staff, such as a head teacher or finance director.

questions.a: A phishing message aimed at one person, using personal details to look convincing

questions.q: A text message says a parcel is held and asks you to pay a fee. What is this?

stations.name: What to do
facts: Don't click links or open attachments in suspicious messages.
Check with the organisation using a number or address you already know.
Report it: to the teacher, the IT team, or a national reporting service.
If you did click, change your password straight away and tell someone.
stations.challenge: Write the three steps you would take if you thought you had been phished.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Don't click links or open attachments in suspicious messages.
Also credit: Check with the organisation using a number or address you already know.

questions.q: You get an email asking you to confirm your password. What should you do?
questions.a: Don't click. Check with the organisation using contact details you already trust

questions.q: You clicked a phishing link and typed your password. What's the first thing to do?
questions.a: Change that password immediately, and any account that shares it

final.name: Final challenge: phish or safe?

questions.q: Is each feature a phishing warning sign, or normal for a genuine message?
questions.a: 'Dear customer, your account will be closed in 24 hours' = Phishing sign; An email address like support@bank-verify.co = Phishing sign; A link that goes to bank.co.uk.secure-login.ru = Phishing sign; A receipt from a shop you used yesterday, with your name on it = Normal; An unexpected attachment called invoice.exe = Phishing sign; A newsletter you signed up for, with an unsubscribe link = Normal; A message asking you to reply with your password = Phishing sign; A school email from a teacher's usual address about homework = Normal

final.note: Students should have predicted these on the worksheet before tapping the star. Mark the prediction, not just the final answer.

exam.q: Describe what phishing is and what the attacker is trying to obtain.
points: Spear phishing targets one person, using details about them to look convincing.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 3.

exam.q: Give two features of a message that suggest it is phishing.
points: The message pretends to come from a trustworthy organisation, such as a bank or a school.
Spear phishing targets one person, using details about them to look convincing.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 2.

exam.q: Explain two measures an organisation can take to reduce the risk of staff being phished.
points: The message pretends to come from a trustworthy organisation, such as a bank or a school.
A way into an organisation's network, by stealing a staff login.
Whaling targets senior staff, such as a head teacher or finance director.
Check with the organisation using a number or address you already know.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 4.

common: Naming a term without saying what it does: most questions need the term and its purpose.
Answering 'it's faster' or 'it's better' with no reason: link it to the characteristic the question is about.
Repeating the question in the answer and stopping there.
